response_text:
Looking at this PR carefully, I need to analyze the multiprocessed flusher implementation, focusing on the backpressure logic, memory checks, default values, and tests.

Key concerns I identified:

1. The default `--flusher-processes=1` contradicts the PR's stated goal of "one process per redis shard"
2. The memory backpressure check now sums across multiple SpansBuffer instances, which could double-count global Redis memory
3. The new test doesn't actually verify flushing works with shared processes
4. Dead code and edge cases in parameter handling
5. Non-deterministic test timing

The factory falls back to `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing 0 would auto-scale but the CLI default of 1 silently disables the new behavior. findings.title: --flusher-processes default of 1 contradicts PR goal
findings.body: The CLI option defaults to 1 and the help text reads 'Defaults to 1'. With `flusher_processes=1` the flusher remains a single process handling all assigned shards, exactly matching the prior behavior and contradicting the PR description 'make the flusher spawn a process per redis shard'. The factory falls back to `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so passing 0 would auto-scale but the CLI default of 1 silently disables the new behavior. The default should be 0 (auto), or the help text/help should clearly indicate operators must opt in to get the multi-process behavior described.

findings.title: max_processes=0 falls through to len(assigned_shards) via `or`
findings.body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy, so callers that explicitly pass 0 (a common sentinel meaning 'auto/unbounded') get silently coerced to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. While 0 is not currently exposed via the CLI default (which is 1), this is a footgun for any future caller (and for the planned 'auto' default). It also makes the check indistinguishable from `None`. Use an explicit `if max_processes is None` check.

findings.title: Memory backpressure check likely over-aggregates Redis global memory
findings.body: In the old single-buffer code, `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` returned one set of Redis memory stats. The new code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` and sums `used`/`available` across all of them. Because every SpansBuffer in `self.buffers` queries the same underlying Redis cluster, each call returns the same global `used`/`available` values; summing N copies multiplies the apparent memory by N. With the new default of N flushers (one per shard), the threshold would trip at roughly `max_memory_percentage / N` of real usage, causing the consumer to hard-pause way before Redis is actually full. Either aggregate once (deduplicating per Redis cluster) or change `get_memory_info` to report per-shard stats before summing.

findings.title: Per-process backpressure raises on any one process, halting the consumer
findings.body: The old code had a single `backpressure_since` for the lone flusher process; raising MessageRejected on that flag paused the consumer for the whole pipeline. The new code raises MessageRejected if *any* one of the per-process backpressure flags is over threshold. With the new shard-per-process layout a single hot shard can now trip backpressure and stop ingestion entirely, even when the other shards have plenty of headroom. The original code also fetched the `backpressure-seconds` option only when needed; the new code fetches it on every submit (small perf regression). Consider only signalling backpressure when *all* processes are stuck, or aggregating by Redis instance.

findings.title: Dead method _create_process_for_shard defined but never called
findings.body: The new code defines `def _create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` with logic that looks up which process owns a shard and restarts that process. It is never invoked from anywhere in the module (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly via `_ensure_processes_alive`). It is misleading dead code that should be removed or actually wired into per-shard restart paths.

findings.title: test_basic relies on time.sleep(0.1) for flusher to drain
findings.body: The test was changed to add an unconditional `time.sleep(0.1)` between setting `current_drift` and `step.join()`. With `produce_to_pipe` set, the flusher now runs as a thread whose loop has a `time.sleep(1)` (defanged by the monkeypatch to `lambda _: None`) and is gated by `stopped.value` only being set in `join()`. The 0.1s sleep is a band-aid for a race: if the thread is not yet past the `buffer.flush_segments` call when `join()` runs, the test fails with no messages. The test should deterministically wait for the flusher (e.g., poll on a counter or a barrier) instead of relying on wall time, and the change from `@pytest.mark.django_db` to `@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)` should be justified in a comment.

findings.title: test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify shared-process flushing works
findings.body: The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that `sum(len(shards) for shards in ... ) == 4`. It does not actually send any spans through `submit()`, so the multi-process/sharing code path (round-robin shard distribution, per-shard SpansBuffer instances, per-process backpressure/health values, per-shard metric tags) is never exercised. Add a case that submits spans into shards handled by each of the two threads and asserts each produced its expected message with the correct `shard` tag.

findings.title: Thread flusher not joined on shutdown when produce_to_pipe is set
findings.body: In `join()`, the loop waits for `process.is_alive()` to become False and then only calls `process.terminate()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. For the test path (`produce_to_pipe is not None`), the workers are `threading.Thread` daemons, so they have no `terminate()`. The code only signals them via `stopped.value`, but the main loop may exit before the thread observes the flag (especially with the monkeypatched `time.sleep`). Daemon threads will be killed when the interpreter exits, but in-process this can leak work in-flight in Redis (e.g., `done_flush_segments` not called), leaving dangling 'flushing' segment keys. Consider an explicit thread shutdown with a small bounded wait, or document the test-only restriction.

findings.title: Inner join loop ignores remaining_time after first wait
findings.body: Inside `join()`, the per-process loop computes `remaining_time = deadline - time.time()` once before the `while process.is_alive()` loop, but never recomputes `deadline` inside that inner loop. After each `time.sleep(0.1)` the comparison `deadline > time.time()` is still correct (it uses absolute deadline), so the loop does terminate, but the initial `remaining_time` check is dead — it is computed and then never consulted again. Harmless but confusing; either remove the pre-check or actually use it to cap the total per-process wait.
